records.name: Ako
records.facts_used: Ako: Linguist Pauls Balodis lists Ako among the Livonian names known from the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia and, following earlier research, treats it as a possible diminutive formed with -o; the root and meaning remain unknown. He also notes that Estonian Ako appeared in a calendar as early as 1845 and was linked there with Ago, a short form of Agathon or August(us), so a modern route from Estonia is also possible. Modern Latvian bearers therefore need not all follow one route. The chronicle names the Livonian leader Ako, who fell during the Livonian resistance at Salaspils in 1206. In a 2024 article for Latvian Public Broadcasting, scholar Janīna Kursīte quotes the chronicle’s report that his head was sent to the bishop with news of victory. This is a historical bearer, not proof that modern Latvian Ako names continue his name directly.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Balodis, Personal Names of Livonian Origin in Latvia (in Names in Multi-Lingual, -Cultural and -Ethnic Contact), PDF pp. 6 and 8: Ako among possible -o diminutives (after Halling and Joalaid 2007); chronicle X:8 chieftain; Estonian Ako in calendar 1845 linked with Ago (Rajandi 1966); possible Estonian route. Root unknown, kept explicit. LSM 11 January 2024 (Kursīte): chronicle quote on head sent to bishop; 1206 Salaspils resistance. The article treats the stone-head identification as speculative; that identification was not used.

records.name: Ēvija
records.facts_used: Ēvija: The Latvian Language Agency’s rendering database gives Swedish Evy as Ēvija, with a long ē. Behind the Name explains Evy as a diminutive of Eva or Evelina, so the name can go back to either of these names. The same database renders Norwegian Evy as Evija with a short e, so the long vowel belongs specifically to the Swedish rendering. The Swedish Evy → Ēvija correspondence comes from Ingrīda Balode’s chapter in the 2003 Latvian handbook on rendering Danish, Norwegian, Swedish and Finnish proper names (p. 327). This is a dated language-standard record, not the first birth registration of Ēvija in Latvia or proof that every bearer’s name came from Swedish.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: LVA search: Swedish Evy → Ēvija (Balode 2003 p. 327); Norwegian Evy → Evija (2003 p. 223); English Avie → Evija (Ahero 2006 p. 93). BTN Evy: diminutive of Eva or Evelina. Rendering record, not first birth.

records.name: Evijs
records.facts_used: Evijs: Klāvs Siliņš’s dictionary of Latvian personal names lists Evijs under Evija, and Evija in turn under Eva. Eva goes back to Hebrew Ḥawwā, explained in the dictionary as ‘life, giver of life’. The dictionary thus places Evijs as a masculine name in the Eva family, but it does not say how the masculine form first arose. The same dictionary records Evijs in Riga in 1971. This is a dated record of use in the dictionary’s material, not necessarily the first Evijs in Latvia.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš catalogue rechecked: Evijs under Evija, Evija under Eva (Ḥawwā); Riga 1971. The dictionary’s own cross-reference is treated as the bridge; no claim about who created the masculine form.

records.name: Atalija
records.facts_used: Atalija: The Lithuanian Universal Encyclopaedia uses Atalija for the biblical Athaliah (Athalyah), queen of Judah. Behind the Name explains the Hebrew name as possibly meaning ‘Yahweh is exalted’. The biblical identification is documented, while the literal meaning remains only probable. According to the encyclopaedia, Athaliah ruled Judah in about 842/841–834 BC, and her story is told in Jean Racine’s tragedy Athalie (1691). The 1964 Lithuanian church calendar reprinted in Antanas Salys’s collected works (1983) lists Atalija on 3 December. These are a biblical-literary example and a calendar record, not proof of when Lithuanian families first used the name.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: VLE Atalija: Athalyah, queen of Judah 842/841–834 BC, Racine Athalie 1691. BTN Athaliah: possibly ‘Yahweh is exalted’. Salys PDF p. 318 / printed p. 303: 3 December Atalija (Ata). The guide’s Greek-city proposal was not re-verified this round and is not used.

records.name: Leiger
records.facts_used: Leiger: Julius Mägiste’s 1929 book Eestipäraseid isikunimesid proposes Leiger as a male given name, comparing Wiedemann’s dictionary word leiger, ‘big strong man, giant’, and the Leiger of Estonian mythology. M. J. Eisen’s Tõll ja ta sugu only conditionally supposes that the giant’s name came from Swedish lekare, ‘player, musician’. The common word and the folklore figure are documented, but the ultimate source of the word is not settled. Mägiste marks Leiger with his abbreviation for his own name proposals, so the 1929 list documents a deliberate proposal rather than an inherited given name. In December 2005 the Suure-Jaani newspaper Leole listed Leiger among December name-day names and called him a hero of the Hiiumaa people. Neither publication proves when a child first received the name.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Mägiste 1929 PDF p. 36 / printed p. 34 visually checked: Leiger (Mg.), cf. Wd. leiger ‘grosser, starker Mann, Riese’, mythology Leiger. PDF p. 12: Mg. = author’s own name proposals. Eisen Tõll ja ta sugu PDF p. 138 conditional Swedish lekare (prior round check reused). Leole Dec 2005 p. 1 rechecked: unqualified lekare claim not adopted.

records.name: Vudro
records.facts_used: Vudro: Siliņš’s dictionary treats Vudro as the Latvian rendering of English Woodrow and cites Old English wudu, forest, and rāw, row, allowing meanings such as a settlement in the forest or a clearing. Behind the Name explains the source surname through a place name meaning a row of houses by a wood. These are alternative readings of the English place-name origin, not one secure literal meaning. The dictionary records Vudro in 1932 and mentions U.S. President Woodrow Wilson in connection with the name. Behind the Name adds that Woodrow became popular in the United States during Wilson’s candidacy and presidency (1912–1921). The 1932 record documents use in Latvia; it does not prove that every family chose the name because of Wilson.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Siliņš p. 333 via catalogue: Woodrow rendering, wudu/rāw, alternative meanings, 1932, Wilson mentioned. BTN Woodrow: row of houses by a wood; popularity 1912–1921. Alternatives kept.

records.name: Vainotas

The 1964 Lithuanian calendar reprinted in Salys’s collected works (1983) lists Vainotas, with the short form Vainas, on 4 December. This is a dated calendar record, not the first use of the name.

records.name: Svaigaudas
records.facts_used: Svaigaudas: Antanas Salys classifies Svaigaudas as an Old Prussian personal name. He links the first element with Old Prussian swais, ‘own’, and the second element gaud- with Lithuanian gauti, ‘to get’, comparing (su)gaudinti. This is an element analysis, not a ready-made translation of the whole name. Salys’s list of name elements, published in his collected works in 1983, gives Svaigaudas among Prussian names under both Svai- and Gaud-. The publication date belongs to the reprinted scholarly list; it does not date the name’s historical use or its adoption in modern Lithuanian calendars.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Salys PDF p. 295 / printed p. 280: Svai-: Prussian swais ‘savas’, Pr. Svaigaudas; PDF p. 287 / printed p. 272: Gaud-: gauti, cf. (su)gaudinti, Pr. Svaigaudas. Not in the 5 December 1964 calendar list (Gratas, Krispina, Sabas, Alanta, Vintilas); publication 1983 only.

records.name: Selma
records.facts_used: Selma: Behind the Name considers the meaning unknown: Selma may be a short form of Anselma, or it may have been inspired by James Macpherson’s Ossian poems, where Selma is the name of a castle. Gulbrand Alhaug’s signed article in the Great Norwegian Encyclopedia describes the same literary source and also mentions the Anselma route. The two routes can both apply, so the name has no single proven meaning. According to Alhaug, Macpherson’s Ossian poems were published in 1761–1763, and Selma came into use as a given name in Germany from the late eighteenth century. In December 2005 the Suure-Jaani newspaper Leole listed Selma among December name-day names. These records concern the name’s European spread and local calendar use, not the first Estonian bearer.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence with explicitly documented alternatives plus one dated record supports two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: BTN Selma: meaning unknown, Anselma or Ossian. SNL Alhaug (fetched): Ossian 1761–1763, German use from late 18th c., Anselma route. Leole Dec 2005 p. 1 lists Selma/Selme with a Gaelic gloss, not adopted.

records.name: Nika
records.facts_used: Nika: Siliņš’s dictionary records feminine and masculine Nika separately. The feminine name is listed under Nikolajs and Greek nikē, victory; the masculine name is also listed under Nikolajs. The dictionary records masculine Nika in Irbe in 1857, with 1889 as its calendar year, and feminine use in 1969 and 1973. The Latvian Language Agency also renders Croatian feminine Nika as Nika, citing Ojārs Bušs’s 2011 article on Croatian names. records.name: Rait
records.facts_used: Rait: Wiktionary’s Estonian entry derives Rait either from the Estonian word rait, ‘colossus’, or as a variant of Raimond. Julius Mägiste’s 1929 list of Estonian personal names includes Rait and tentatively compares it with Raik. The available sources keep these routes open rather than choosing one. Mägiste cites a historical record of the form Rayth from a sixteenth-century Polish survey of Livonia, published in the series Polska XVI wieku. This is an old personal-name record cited in a 1929 scholarly list, not proof that every modern Rait continues that name directly.
